extracted.intended_audience: scholars, economists, and policymakers focused on patent policy and USPTO administration
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical and simulation analysis estimating the savings and costs of increasing patent examiner time allocations (e.g., doubling time). Uses examiner GS-level variation to identify effects on litigation, PTAB challenges, and prosecution rounds and compares those savings to personnel and administrative costs to the Patent Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification strategy using GS-level variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow examiners through promotions that change GS-levels (and thereby change time allocations) and observe impacts on application outcomes while controlling for other factors (e.g., experience). Use GS-level differences (e.g., GS-14 relative to GS-7) as the source of variation in examination time to estimate causal effects of increased examiner time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret GS-level coefficients relative to a baseline (e.g., the GS-level 14 coefficient interpreted with reference to a GS-level 7 effect). Note statistical challenges: GS-level relationships may be noisy (PTAB events are rare), there can be non-monotonic patterns (e.g., a spike at GS-11), and PTAB challenges only began after September 2012 which reduces observed incidence over the sample period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure effect on PTAB challenge incidence (normalized incidence rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate how changes in examination time affect the number of times a patent application becomes the subject of a PTAB challenge (up to March 2016). Example finding: the normalized incidence rate of PTAB activity at GS-level 14 is roughly 3.55 relative to the baseline incidence rate of 1.0 for GS-level 7; moving examiners from GS-14 to GS-7 (doubling their time) implies a roughly 72% (2.55/3.55) reduction in PTAB challenge frequency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because PTAB is rarer than litigation and only effective since late 2012, PTAB-based estimates are expected to be somewhat noisier; consider these features when interpreting incidence-rate estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute total PTAB savings by multiplying reductions by average PTAB litigation costs
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute total PTAB expense savings, multiply the predicted reduction in the number of instituted PTAB petitions by the average litigation costs associated with PTAB proceedings, derived from AIPLA Annual Survey data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked example (Table 4): 430,056 annual disposals × mean PTAB challenges 0.00088 ⇒ roughly 378 instituted PTAB petitions; doubling examination time predicted to reduce this by 72% (≈272 fewer instituted petitions). Multiply 272 by average PTAB litigation cost (from AIPLA) ⇒ $123,080,000 in gross savings (before discounting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate timing and discounting for PTAB savings
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the lag between patent issuance and onset of PTAB proceedings when converting lump-sum savings into annualized values. Using patents issued in 2012, the average lag between issuance and PTAB onset is estimated at 2.1 years; assume the bulk of PTAB expenses are incurred one year after PTAB filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discount the $123M gross savings by 3.1 years. Using a 3% discount rate yields annual savings ≈ $112M; at 7% discount rate yields ≈ $100M. Explicitly state discount rate and lag assumptions when reporting annualized savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for baseline rarity and noise in PTAB estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that PTAB challenges are less frequent than litigation and occurred only after September 2012, thus reducing mean incidence and increasing statistical difficulty in estimating impacts of GS-level changes on PTAB frequencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect greater statistical noise and less precise estimates; report uncertainty and note any non-monotonicities (e.g., unusual spikes by GS-level). Consider restricting samples or using robustness checks to address truncation and timing issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual tradeoff for prosecution costs per applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing examiner time could reduce prosecution rounds by producing clearer rejections (saving applicant costs) or could increase per-round complexity (e.g., more complex obviousness rejections with many references) thus raising applicant costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically test both margins: (1) whether more examiner time reduces the number of office actions/rounds of review, and (2) whether more time increases the complexity and per-round cost of office actions. Explicitly acknowledge theoretical ambiguity and assess both directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical test of rounds-of-review effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the same GS-level promotion identification to test whether more examination time reduces the number of rounds (office actions) associated with applications. Preferred specification result: doubling examination time is associated with 0.56 fewer rounds of review per application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate reduction in rounds into dollar savings by assuming a per-round cost (the analysis assumes modest-complexity rounds cost $2,500). Multiply per-round cost × reduction in rounds × annual disposals (≈430,000) ⇒ gross savings estimate (example: $602M). Report assumptions and sample/clustering controls and subject estimates to robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for changes in per-office-action attorney fees (natural experiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit the 2010 USPTO two-hour increase (≈12% increase) as a natural experiment: compare median attorney charges before and after (AIPLA 2008, 2010, 2012) across technology/complexity cells to identify whether increased examiner time led to higher per-office-action fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed result: median attorney fees for responding to an examiner’s rejection stayed flat or decreased from 2008 to 2012. Caveats: other market factors (law firm mergers, economic conditions) could confound results; small time increases may not scale linearly to effects from doubling time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative adjustment / discounting of prosecution savings
rubrics_metrics.description: Given methodological concerns (limitations of the natural experiment and robustness around the 0.56 estimate), apply conservative discounts to gross prosecution-savings estimates when used in aggregate cost-benefit calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: halve the $602M gross prosecution-savings estimate to a conservative $301M for use in the paper’s central cost-benefit calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit scope of simulation to quantifiable savings (litigation, PTAB, prosecution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to quantify broader welfare harms from invalid patents (e.g., monopoly deadweight loss, impediments to follow-on innovation, venture-capital deterrence) due to difficulties in reliable quantification; focus simulation analysis on litigation, PTAB, and prosecution expense savings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge existence of other social harms (supracompetitive pricing, NPE opportunism, inhibited follow-on research) and cite empirical literature (Galasso & Schankerman; Sampat & Williams) but exclude hard-to-quantify channels from the numerical simulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AIPLA survey data for cost inputs and complexity cells
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw attorney-fee and litigation-cost inputs from the AIPLA Annual Survey (median charges by technology and complexity). Define 'minimal complexity' (e.g., ten-page specification and ten claims) per AIPLA definitions when mapping costs to rounds of review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the AIPLA source, relevant table rows (e.g., Table 5 median charges for 2008/2010/2012), and the technology/complexity cell used for per-round cost assumptions; discuss whether the chosen complexity cell is conservative/representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for Patent Office budget response scenarios when estimating costs
rubrics_metrics.description: When increasing examiner time, consider two institutional responses: (1) fixed USPTO budget → must reduce number of applications processed (longer pendency/backlog) with social costs from delay and reputational harm; or (2) increase budget and hire more examiners → primary costs are personnel expenses for additional examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both social costs (backlog effects: reduction in value to applicants, deterrence to innovation, diversion of resources; see London Econ. estimate) and administrative feasibility. The paper assumes the USPTO would maintain production by increasing budget (user-fee adjustments), therefore focusing on personnel costs as the primary cost category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate cost accounting assumption: maintain production
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceed under the assumption that the Patent Office would maintain its examination production level in the face of increased per-application review time by augmenting its budget and hiring additional examiners; therefore, aggregate costs associated with increased time allocation are primarily personnel expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make this explicit when computing net benefits: if instead the USPTO froze budget and reduced throughput, the relevant social costs would differ (mainly delays/backlog). State this assumption clearly and explore sensitivity to alternative institutional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report key simulation quantities and intermediate calculations transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the intermediate quantities used in simulations (e.g., number of annual disposals 430,056; mean PTAB challenges 0.00088; predicted reduction 72%; predicted fewer instituted petitions 272; gross PTAB savings $123,080,000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the structure paralleling other tables (e.g., Table 3 for litigation savings), state the data sources for each input (AIPLA, USPTO disposals, sample periods), and document any sample restrictions or alternative sample choices (e.g., post-AIA only) and their effects.
